subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I interrupted my speech yesterday at five o'clock, I was saying it might be appropriate to provide a few historical notes. During the fifties and sixties, there were many complaints because
August 25, 1987

Canadians felt that the price of drugs was too high. Eventually, the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission held an inquiry on the manufacture, distribution and sale of drugs, under Section 42 of the Combines Investigation Act. 1 can assure the House that this was an exhaustive inquiry and that the recommendations contained in the report subsequently published by the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission were quite significant. I shall quote the findings of the inquiry.
Consideration should be given to the establishment, under the auspices of the federal government, of an authoritative publication giving all necesary particulars concerning new drugs-
As the Commission believes that close control exercised by patents has made it possible to maintain prices of certain drugs at level higher than would have obtained otherwise and that such patent control has produced no benefits to the public of Canada which would outweigh the disadvantages of the monopoly, the Commission recommends that patents with respect to drugs be abolished. In the opinion of the Commission this is the only effective remedy to reduce the price of drugs in Canada.
We must remember that the government's decision at the end of the sixties to amend the Patent Act was made following an inquiry conducted by the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission which had clearly ruled that the price of drugs in Canada at the time was too high and that steps had to be taken to force the companies to reduce the price of drugs in Canada. This means that people were aware of the high prices of drugs that enjoyed patent protection and that at the time, these prices were judged to be too high.
In fact, other studies made at the time as well reached the same conclusion. A Joint Committee of the House of Commons and the Senate made a similar study and reached the same conclusions, and so the Government's action followed recommendations made by the competent authorities whose duty it is to determine competition levels in Canada, as in the case of the Restrictive Trade Practices commission and a recommendation, unanimous at the time, made by Members and Senators of the Parliament of Canada.
Our present system which sets limits on the rights of companies under the Patent Act was at the time approved unanimously by all political parties in the House and in the Senate.
I have heard some Conservative Members say that we condoned plagiarism, that we let generic drug companies copy the discoveries made by pharmaceutical firms. So we did. So we did, but with the unanimous support of all Members, including the Conservative Members who sat in this House in the late 1960s. There was one basic reason why the system was set up: we wanted to make sure that the already inflated drug prices in Canada would decline.
To the Conservative Members who maintain that certain countries enforce regulations to protect inventors of pharmaceutical products for 17 years and even more, my response is that in such countries as England, France and a few other European countries the drug companies may indeed be better protected than our own Canadian firms, but then these companies are subject to much stricter price controls.
Patent Act
Unfortunately the federal Government has no authority to enforce price controls because they come under provincial jurisdiction. When we are told that the patents of a drug company in France are protected over a much longer period of time than is the case here in Canada, I say fair enough, but you conveniently forget to point out that this drug company simply cannot market its products unless it has reached an agreement with government authorities concerning a fair price which will enable it to earn a fair return on its investment, a fair profit.
What we in the Liberal Opposition are concerned about right now is that Canada does not have any control over drug prices. So we are going back to the old system. To put it another way, the Government has decided to bring us back to those days when drug companies were much better protected than they are now, to the extent that they would not have to face competition from Canadian generic drug companies before ten years.
Well, we believe that this ten-year protection is excessive under the circumstances, the more so because there is nothing in the Bill to guarantee that the companies will keep their prices at an affordable and reasonable level for consumers.
Unless it is amended along the line of the proposals put forward by Liberal Senators, this Bill will be toothless. It will have no power to compel pharmaceutical companies to keep their promises, namely to make investments, to create jobs and especially to keep drug prices at levels which are affordable and reasonable for Canadian consumers generally. Well, this Government would like us to trust blindly the pharmaceutical companies and positively give them "carte blanche" for the next 10 years, without really knowing whether they will do any actual research in Canada, create as many jobs as they say they will and especially maintain reasonable prices.
We feel that the Minister, regardless of his good will, is placing himself in a position of vulnerability with respect to the pharmaceutical industry, because his Bill lacks the means to force these companies to deliver. And that is what makes the whole difference with this Government which wants to amend the Patent Act to allow the pharmaceutical companies to benefit more from their research and earn a higher return from their investments.
We fully agree on the need to amend the Act to make it possible for these companies to recover at least their investments. But we just cannot agree on this excessive protection. There was a commission of inquiry and Professor Eastman, who examined this matter thoroughly, found that a four-year protection was quite sufficient. As a conclusion, Mr. Speaker, 1 ask again the same question as yesterday: Why does the Government insist on giving these additional six years to the pharmaceutical companies? To what extent does it hope to convince us that these six years are absolutely essential to attract invesments into this country? We feel that the Minister

August 25, 1987
Patent Act
of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) is much too generous with the pharmaceutical companies, while his first responsibility should be to protect Canadian consumers, and not to demonstrate so much generosity towards the pharmaceutical companies. It is all right to amend the legislation to allow for a fair return on their investments, but not to give them "carte blanche" to grow fat and rich at the expense of Canadian consumers during the last six years of protection they would enjoy under this Bill.
Those who think that the Liberal party is against investment in the Montreal area are greatly mistaken. We support investment by drug companies in the Montreal area. It is indeed because we support that kind of investment that we want the legislation to be quite clear and binding. It is not. The companies may in the first months of the new system invest some funds in research, but there is nothing in the legislation that compels them to carry on their efforts in the area of research during the 10 following years, during which they will be given a protection that in our opinion is very generous, even too generous and dangerous for Canadian consumers. This is why 1 hope that the Government in its wisdom will reconsider that decision and will accept the amendments that were proposed in good faith in the interests of Canadian consumers by the Liberal senators.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister; Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for giving me the opportunity to make a few comments. It is always a surprise to hear the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet), who had no qualms telling us, and I quote: "We support investment in the Montreal area". I find no word to characterize, 1 see no logic in that way of thinking . . . Although I have been trying over these last few months to follow the logic of the Official Opposition on that issue, I have not succeeded yet.
When we refer to creating new jobs in the Montreal area, and this is what my comments will deal with, we referred to 1,300 jobs because we banked on the jobs that were guaranteed to us by the companies. And this they did not tell us behind close doors-they did so officially, they said it to newspapers, they made a commitment. And as I read in Le Devoir economique . . . Drug industry people in the Montreal area are not referring to 1,300 jobs, they are expecting up to 10,000 new jobs in the drug industry, to once more give our young Canadian scientists-not only from Quebec but from across Canada an opportunity to work in that industry. This they had been denied for some years. Scientists have to move down to the United States, they must emigrate abroad in order to find work. So they are digging in, they have the gall to suggest we did not put enough teeth in our bill. This in my view is showing a form of bad faith, because it is the first time in more than a decade that a Government decides to take a firm stand in that area and ensure that the Canadian Government is no longer a cowboy, a freelancer in the global drug industry.
This country was operating in a totally opposite direction from other nations in that area. I would understand it if
Members of the Official Opposition remained silent on that, especially those from the Montreal area. If I were in their shoes I would hide in shame. But no, they are here. They are responsible, but they blame us for not fully accepting the Eastman report, as if we should always accept a report that is submitted to us. But in the same breath they reject the Macdonald report, a report chaired by a former Liberal minister who recommends that we increase trade with the United States. There is no logic in that attitude.
I would like to know, Mr. Speaker, how they can openly tell us Quebecers, us Canadians, that preventing those kinds of investment to be made soon in the Montreal area, those brains . .. Certainly the Hon. Member has young children as 1 have. We must provide work for them. There is work now in various fields, but in the industrial sector, in the high technology, in research and development, what do they have to suggest to stimulate research and development in the Montreal area? For our part, we do not merely have an assumption, but a confirmed assurance. People in the Montreal area-not politicians, but the entire medical profession expect some ten thousand jobs. I will conclude my comments with that.
My question is as follows: What do they have to suggest? What guarantee do they have? They told us that the first budget of this Government would result in the loss of 200,000 jobs and after less than three years, 900,000 jobs have been created. What is their logic? How can we believe those people? What is your position? What is your answer? What do you have to offer to the Montreal area?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find such demagogy regrettable on the part of the Parliamentary Secretary as it clearly shows his ignorance.
These are the facts. The Patent Act was amended to allow compulsory licencing because drug prices were higher in Canada than anywhere else in the world. When this legislation was passed, it was passed not only by the then Liberal Government, but also with the unanimous consent of all Conservative Members of Parliament.
The Liberals are therefore not to blame for developing in Canada a new system which was certainly different from other systems in the world. The Government had the courage at the time to tell the pharmaceutical multinationals: We have had enough, you are exploiting the Canadian people by selling your drugs at excessive prices.
We developed a system to protect the Canadian consumers. The pharmaceutical companies are now saying: We are willing to create jobs and to invest more in research in Canada if you remove the compulsory licencing system. As for us, we are saying that we are willing to accept this offer and provide the guarantees and protection which the drug companies say they need to make these investments. However, in return, we want the companies to make some firm commitments and we want them to keep these commitments.
August 25, 1987

As for the Parliamentary Secretary, he is willing to trust blindly in the pharmaceutical companies even though they exploited consumers in the past. There is no clear stipulation in the bill that these investments will take place or that the pharmaceutical companies will maintain reasonable prices and not bring about excessive price increases as they did in the past.
The Parliamentary Secretary says that he wants a system which will allow the pharmaceutical companies to invest more in the Montreal region, and I quite agree with him. 1 would like the pharmaceutical companies to invest more in research in Montreal. However, the world situation is such that the Canadian market is very small compared with the American and European markets, and the fact is that the pharmaceutical multinationals carry out their research in well-established centres. Much of this work is now carried out in Puerto Rico, where it costs much less to operate, and via Puerto Rico, the multinationals have free access to the American market. The pharmaceutical companies have also moved much of their operations to Ireland, where they have obtained major concessions, because of which they can operate at a very low cost and have access to the European market.
It does not take long to realize that Canada is not in the same position as Ireland and Puerto Rico, and that whatever research can be carried out in Canada will be minimal compared with world research in pharmaceutical products, unless the text of the legislation contains specific guarantees to force the companies to do research in Canada and create jobs.
This is what we are asking, and this is what the Bill does not do.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in this debate. 1 shall not speak any longer than necessary this morning to Bill C-22, since my Conservative colleagues have already spoken on the subject, and I may refer more particlar-ly ot the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre), who was eloquent, as always, in his speech last Friday. My colleagues have already put forward a number of arguments, all of which are extremly convincing and favour the passage of Bill C-22 as proposed by the Government.
Mr. Speaker, I shall not repeat all these arguments, but nevertheless, I wish to add my voice to those that are urging the House and especially the Senate to adopt this important piece of legislation as soon as possible, for the sake of the thousands of jobs that would result, jobs whose future is now being threatened by Opposition Members who refuse to listen to reason, and why, I frankly don't know. We are ready to accept constructive criticism, but when we have an Opposition that criticizes for partisan purposes, and that is particularly
Patent Act
true of the non-elected Liberals in the Senate, that we cannot accept.
Mr. Speaker, I would now like to refer to a specific case that has strengthened my personal convictions in favour of Bill C-22, and it is the case of Hoffmann-La Roche whose now vacant buildings are located in my own riding of Vaudreuil.
The history of this case reflects the devastating impact that, slowly but surely, the Liberal Government's amendments to the Patent Act of 1969 have had, an intolerable situation, Mr. Speaker, that our Government is now actively trying to improve. I would like to quote, in passing, a few paragraphs from an editorial by Albert Juneau published in Le Devoir this morning. I am using this particular editorial, Mr. Speaker, because it happened to appear this morning, but I could quote from many others published in recent months. 1 quote:
The Liberal Senators have launched their defence of the average consumer with unusual zeal, in their parliamentary skirmishes against Bill C-22 concerning drug patents. Their partisan tactics fool no one but say a great deal about the state of health of the Liberal Party and the Upper Chamber-
Through their exaggerated juxtaposition of the foreign multinationals, especially the U.S. companies, and the poor Canadian consumers, the Liberals are undermining the debate and ignoring what is really at stake.
The basic principle underlying Bill C-22 is that drug patents should again be issued with ownership rights similar to those which prevail in other major industrialized countries. Back in 1969, the Liberal administration had brought in an important amendment under which protection granted new drugs was reduced to a year and a half, whereas our main trading partners kept the widely accepted 17-to-20-year standard. The Government was hoping to force a decline in prices and promote stiffer competition between so-called innovating companies-research and development oriented-and generic medicine manufacturers who "copy" and market the new drugs.
The new legislation increases to seven years the protection period granted any product for which a mandatory licence has been issued (it would be ten years in the case of imported products). For their part the Liberals suggest that the maximum monopoly period be four years and that the current 4 per cent royalty paid by generic manufacturers to research firms be raised to 14 per cent.
It is difficult to understand why the Liberal Senate is fighting tooth and nail against the elected House of Commons to try and gain a few years protection, when impact studies on the Government legislation clearly demonstrate that Canadian consumers will come out winners-
To the industry, especially the innovative companies, this Bill provide incentives for research and development investments. The 1969 amendments did not prove beneficial to Canada which now ranks behind poorer nations such as Italy and the United Kingdom as far as drug research and development is concerned. Quebec, where half of the research and development spending is concentrated in Canada, has severely suffered because of such memorable closings as Ayerst and Hoffmann-LaRoche in 1982. Since then, Quebec scientists and politicians have been unanimous in their efforts to have the legislation amended.
While stubbornly confining themselves to idle chatter, the Liberals are unfairly stopping a Bill which is acceptable both to the consumers and the industry.
In its brief to the chairman of the Eastman Commission created by the former Liberal Government to study the pharmaceutical industry in Canada, Hoffmann-La Roche, or Roche Canada as it is better known, explained in detail how

the 1969 amendments to the Patent Act adversely affected its operations, resulting in the loss of jobs and millions of dollars for research and development in Canada, in the Province of Quebec, and in the riding of Vaudreuil,
The 1969 amendments to the Patent Act under the then Liberal Government had a dramatic impact on the sales of Roche Canada's major pharmaceutical products. Since the beginning of the 1970s Roche Canada's viability steadily deteriorated to the point where it began to incur substantial losses. Indeed, in the early 1980s Roche Canada lost millions of dollars on its operations. Management therefore decided that massive and immediate cost reduction measures had to be instituted to stop the ever increasing deficits. One of those cost reduction measures announced in November, 1982, consisted of the complete and permanent closure of the company's plant in Vaudreuil, Quebec, effective in the summer of 1983.
The closure of Roche Canada's Vaudreuil operation resulted in the loss of close to 80 manufacturing jobs and about the same number of related jobs. The reduction in Roche Canada's activity led to a corresponding reduction in its contribution to the Canadian economy as a whole. This is of course not to mention the very severe economic impact on the local economy of my riding and its surroundings.

But let us return to the here and now, Mr. Speaker. Another article, which appeared last fall in the Le Devoir economique section, foresaw the creation of 10,000 jobs in the Montreal area due to the direct and indirect economic fallouts from Bill C-22. Mr. Speaker, how could we understand and accept the bickering from non-elected Liberals in the Senate when a great many prestigious groups and personalities both in Quebec and the rest of Canada are urging the Government to go ahead with its Bill? I refer among others to Quebec Premier Robert Bourassa, to Mayor Jean Dore, to the Armand Frappier Institute, to the School of Medicine of the Montreal, Sherbrooke and McGill universities, the Federation of General Practioners of Quebec, as well as a great many others, Mr. Speaker.
As the member for Vaudreuil I support the immediate passage of Bill C-22 as introduced by the Government. Several innovative pharmaceutical companies are located in my Vaudreuil constituency and nearby ridings, including the Dollard and Lachine constituencies, and they provide a great many jobs which, in turn, bring important economic spinoffs for our region. And those research and development jobs are for our university graduates who have no other choice today than to expatriate themselves, when we could give them the opportunity to work at home and make people around them benefit from both the economic spinoffs and the impact of their research which we need for reasons fully explained previously. We cannot do without the millions of dollars in investment and jobs which will be created in our region with the passage of Bill C-22. And by region, I mean of course more particularly the Vaudreuil area, but also the province of
Quebec and the entire country. 1 therefore encourage all those who want to prevent the passage of the bill to stop and finally listen to reason.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Labour, who is an honest and conscientious Member of the House, would certainly not leave on the official report of our Debates statements which are absolutely unfounded.
He has just made two. First, he claimed that the 1962 legislation was the reason behind the closing in his riding by the Hoffmann-La Roche Corporation of their Vaudreuil facilities. That was only an excuse! No impartial observer in Canada would claim that this is the real reason why this company decided to leave. It was just an excuse. It was a decision made in a particular context and which was used by the company to comply with a management decision taken outside Canada. Those who were working for this company in Canada did not want the plant to close. Such decisions made by multinationals abroad affect the economy and the labour situation in Canada.
When we rely exclusively on multinationals for the economic survival of our country, we are most vulnerable, and there are situations such as that one where business executives residing outside Canada make decisions which have serious consequences for the Canadian economy.
Unfortunately, this Bill has not enough teeth to ensure that decisions such as those made in the past by business bosses abroad would not be repeated.
The other thing I should like to bring to the Minister's attention is a statement made by Sir John A. Macdonald, the first Conservative Leader of his Party, and I quote:
There would be no use of an upper House if it did not exercise, when it thought proper, the right of opposing or amending or postponing the legislation of the lower House. It would be of no value whatever were it a mere chamber for registering the decrees of the lower House. It must be an independent House, having a free action of its own, for it is only valuable as being a regulating body, calmly considering the legislation initiated by the popular branch, and preventing any hasty or ill-considered legislation which may come from that body.

It is obvious that Sir John A. Macdonald recognized to the Canadian Senate the right to consider a bill introduced in this House and the right to amend the legislation.
Now the Minister of Labour, when suggesting that the Senate is filibustering, is leaving out a step. I hope that he will have the decency of acknowledging that he is anticipating the facts.
The Senate up to now has carried its duty which is to consider a bill from this House and to suggest amendments, as has often been done in the past. The Senate has not yet gone beyond its duty. We are considering a motion to return the bill to the Senate without the amendments which it has proposed.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was not surprised that the Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall), who led off this debate for the Official Opposition, took almost three hours to explain the Liberals' position. After all, they have a lot of explaining to do. It was the Liberals, when they were in Government, in fact the Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet), when he was the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, who opened this whole can of worms.
Let us have a brief history lesson, Mr. Speaker. Until 1969 Canada had the second highest prices for prescription drugs in

August 25, 1987
Patent Act
the world. The only country that had higher prices was the United States. There was a great deal of complaint, very justifiably and understandably. A number of studies were done, and during the Liberal regime a parliamentary committee held lengthy hearings and finally made a report which led to the change in the Patent Act laws in 1969 as they affected prescription drugs.
From 1969 until the present time, instead of having the second highest prescription drug prices in the world we have had among the lowest. The successor to the Hon. Member for Papineau as Minister of Consumer Affairs, Mrs. Erola, who has now taken a very well-paid job as a lobbyist for the multinational drug companies, buckled under to pressure and appointed Professor Eastman to conduct a study. Professsor Eastman conducted that study and reported, fortunately or unfortunately, after the Government had changed and we had a Conservative Government. Professsor Eastman said essentially that the system had worked well, that we had saved the Canadian consumer, either directly or indirectly through public and private prescription drug insurance plans, hundreds of millions of dollars, but that we could improve the system.
He said that we could extend the period for exclusivity for the companies which developed the drugs by a few years, that we could increase the royalties which the generic companies had to pay for the right to produce generic drugs, but that aside from that the system was working quite well.
Instead the Conservative Government buckled under completely to the pressure of the multinational companies and the pressure of President Reagan who made it a condition of even talking about free trade that we change our regulations. The Conservative Government brought in legislation. It ignored almost every important recommendation made by Professor Eastman.
The Minister talks about the support for this Bill. It has some support, about which I will elaborate in a moment, but what the Minister did today and my hon. friend for Dauphin- Swan River (Mr. White) did yesterday was to say that those people who do not support the Bill do not know what they are talking about.
Who are these people who oppose the Bill? It would take me all day to list all the groups and organizations, but I will summarize who they are. They are labour organizations, seniors organizations from one end of Canada to the other, the Consumers' Association of Canada, and farm groups such as Keystone Agriculture in my province of Manitoba which represents all the farmers who produce various commodities except grain. As well, six of the ten provinces told the Government that they have considered its proposal and believe it will cost their pharmacare plans tens of millions of dollars.
Of course, there are some who support the Bill, including some medical researchers. It is not surprising that they support the Bill because they are so starved for research funds that
they are prepared to take funds from anyone who will provide them.
I remind Members of the House that when the Conservatives were in opposition, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) attacked the Liberals, saying that it was unacceptable and inexcusable that we were one of the lowest investors in scientific research and development among the industrialized countries. He promised that when a Conservative Government took office it would move quickly to invest 2.5 per cent of Gross National Product for scientific research and development.
Let us consider what has actually happened. Instead of the 1.9 per cent of GNP that we were spending when the Liberals were in government, we are now spending 1.3 per cent under a Conservative Government that promised to spend twice that amount. Obviously, scientists are moving to the United States. Why would they stay in Canada when there is no work for them and the Government has made it very clear that it will not invest or force the private sector of the economy to invest the kinds of funds which are necessary?
The Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux) talked about Hoffmann-La Roche in his constituency of Vaudreuil. Let me tell the Minister what the Government did to my city of Winnipeg. There was an agreement between the former Liberal Government of Canada and the Province of Manitoba to build a centre in which scientific research could be done in the City of Winnipeg. The agreement was concluded and the building erected. The building is virtually empty because the Conservative Government, in its desire to hold the line and reduce the deficit, cancelled the money for the funding needed to operate the centre.
We must understand a number of points. First, we have heard repeatedly from the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre), and now from the Minister of Labour and the Parliamentary Secretary, about how many jobs will be produced if and when this Bill is passed. There is not a single word in the Bill requiring the companies to produce the jobs that they have promised. There is not a single clause or a single word in the Bill providing penalties for the companies if they do not produce the jobs they have promised. In fact, there is nothing in the Bill that would require any company to do anything. The Bill does not even stipulate that those companies which produce jobs will get benefits and those companies that do not will not get benefits. There is simply a general assumption in the Bill that everything will work. All the organizations and groups which oppose the Bill have said that is unacceptable.
The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs continues to talk about the amounts of money and expenditures on research and development that will be made. The Minister tosses around figures of hundreds of millions of dollars like they were confetti. Yet the figures add up so fast that he is unable to keep track of them. For instance, on August 15 he claimed that $900 million would be invested. That required
August 25, 1987

two additional amounts of $280 million and $130 million to be added to the PMAC figure of $553 million. The figures are meaningless when he can simply pull them out of the air as he sees fit and then threaten that this investment will disappear if the Bill does not pass, as the Minister of Labour said a few moments ago.
It is this combination of promotion and blackmail that tries to obscure the very real issues associated with drug industry research. One does not achieve real basic medical research by spreading the money out in dribs and drabs. Instead, it should be put into establishing a major medical research centre which we do not have.
The pharmaceutical manufacturers themselves have said that it can cost up to $100 million to make a major breakthrough and produce one real new drug that will treat an important illness, such as cancer, heart disease or stroke. Does anyone really believe that in Canada, with our small population of 25 million and a very limited market, any drug company will really invest up to $100 million in the hopes of producing one new drug? That is nonsense. The drug companies will simply continue their past practice of experimenting with a drug to derive a new variation which they can sell in competition with another company and thereby have an edge for a few months or years.
The Government would have us believe that it was only after the 1969 legislation that a situation developed in which it was not profitable for the drug companies to invest in research. Let us consider what happened before 1969 when we did not have this legislation. I challenge anyone on the government side or someone from the drug companies to tell me and Canadians the name of one major drug discovery that was made in Canada before 1969 when, according to the Government and the industry, this terrible legislation destroyed their ability or desire to do research?
There was one major discovery which has saved hundreds of thousands, if not millions of lives. That was the discovery of insulin. Yet lo and behold, insulin was not produced by one of these multinational corporations but was produced in a laboratory of the medical college of the University of Toronto. I suggest to the industry and the Government that if we want real research done in Canada, let us give the universities and scientific community, particularly the university medical and biotechnology researchers, the opportunity to do so.

I wish to deal for a few moments with the question of the supposed inability of these drug companies, these poor drug companies, to do research. I wish to put on the record some of the facts we learned, or should have learned, that appeared in two articles published in The Globe and Mail on August 21 last. The first states in part:
Canadian subsidiaries of multinational pharmaceutical companies are among the most profitable businesses in the country, but taxpayers may end up footing much of the bill for the increased research the companies are promising . . . even under that patent regimen, many of the multinational drug
Patent Act
companies already make a level of profit rarely reported by other Canadian manufacturers.
In a sample for 1983 and 1984-
Their return on shareholders' equity . . . averaged 25 per cent in 1984 and 23 per cent a year earlier, which would put the companies near the top 25 in the Report on Business ranking of 1000 companies.
How much more do we have to give them before they will agree to do anything? The article raises another important question, that is, the whole question of inter-company transfers. The article points out:
The money that multinational drug companies take out of Canada often flows in ways other than the normal dividends a subsidiary pays to its parent.
That is a big figure in itself-in one recent two-year period, 10 companies sampled paid dividends totalling almost $60 million a year, about equal to the industry's Canadian spending on research. But further huge amounts also move through other intercorporate arrangements.
These transfers, which include royalties paid to the parent ($20 million a year in the period studied) and fees paid to the parent ($9.5 million) are a cost of doing business for the subsidiary, and therefore have the effect of reducing profit.
But the biggest factor-and one that Revenue Canada is disputing with some companies-is transfer pricing-
Transfer pricing is a way of shifting money within related companies to move profits out of high-tax areas into more favorable jurisdictions. In a typical transaction, the Canadian subsidiary would pay an offshore affiliate an inflated price for the raw material used to make a prescription drug. This overhigh price becomes a cost to the domestic company, cutting its profit and therefore its tax bill.
I digress for a moment to remind Hon. Members that these are among the most profitable companies in Canada.
In the 10-company sample, eight multinationals' total purchases from related companies totalled more than $250 million a year. The two other companies did not give exact figures, but one said it was "dependent" on a related party and the other said a "majority" of its business was with related companies.
I know that I have just about used up my allotted time, Mr. Speaker. Revenue Canada has been looking into this intercompany transferring for years. In fact, at least one of the companies settled by paying over $650,000 to Revenue Canada. We are talking about very wealthy and powerful companies. They do not need this legislation if they really want to do research. They are already making very high profits. The extent to which we subsidize them must be cut back. We should be doing more for other companies which employ more people, many more people than these companies, and which should be getting help so that they can do research to make them more efficient and better able to deal with competition.

speakeroldname: Hon. Frank Oberle (Minister of State (Science and Technology)):
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I almost missed my turn to debate this issue. On the way from my office I was held up by a large demonstration in front of the Chamber; it is presently ongoing, and Your Honour should be apprised of. There are at least 1,000 young people there who are demanding that politicians who held prominent positions of another age free up the debate of this House and proceed with the passing of this legislation. These young scientists and engineers out there are demanding jobs.
Naturally, as the Minister of State (Science and Technology), I am interested in their message. I am sure you would assume that at one point I would wish to say a few words on Bill C-22 because this debate does concern science and technology. This debate does concern research and development. This debate does concern Canada in the 21st Century. This debate is about using science and technology and research and development to carve a niche for Canada in the new age and to overcome some of the historic problems of regional alienation and a lack of resolve in this critical area of science and technology.
The world is changing in a very dramatic fashion. Some say it is the dawning of a new age. Every single person in our country, every nation in the world, will determine its place in the 21st Century by the way it responds to the challenges and trends which are out there. The socio-economic well-being of entire nations is being determined by what is happening.
I have heard it said that over the next 30 years we will experience as profound a change in our socio-economic conditions in western civilization as we have experienced over the last 200 years of the industrial revolution. Just imagine what that means, Mr. Speaker. Can one even contemplate

August 25, 1987
Patent Act
what that means? How do we respond to this? How do we prepare ourselves for these changes?
We are designing new rules. New norms and standards are being created every day, and each one has to measure his or her own performance, and nations have to measure their performance in accordance with these new rules and the trends that are measurable throughout the world.
Since we pride ourselves on being one of the seven most important industrial nations in the world, we too have to begin to play by the rules which have been established by the people with whom we compare ourselves, by the general rules of the western world of which we are such an important part. Certainly, this Government intends to stay in the fast current, to stay with the leaders, to man the new frontier with the very best, because we have the potential to do that. We have the energies and resources to do it and we shall not disappoint future generations by depriving them of their opportunities to be with the best in the world.
We must compare our performance with those with whom we compete, and they are the best in the world. We must play by the rules we have collectively established. Clearly, what is known at this point is that knowledge, intellectual capital, shall be the currency of that new age. It is no longer the land it was in the agrarian age. It is not energy as it was throughout the industrial revolution. It is knowledge and intellectual capital. The rules that are being established in accordance with the management of this capital, who has the right over it, who can accumulate and who can claim ownership, have already been established in the international market-place.
There are really two sets of rules established. They are not new. Those rules were established in the agrarian revolution and the industrial revolution and they are consistent with the trends we are experiencing now.
Our socialist friends, of course, would like to play by a different set of rules where we have collective farms, collective ownership of capital and the right of the collectivities to manage the economy in a central way. Those are not the rules of the people with whom we compete in the world. They are not the rules of the people with whom we share the responsibility of making the world a better place to live, the western civilization, where private enterprise and private initiative are very important and salient factors.
Our socialist friends have other ideas, and that is understandable. But what is not understandable is the confusion of our Liberal friends. That is not understandable. They lament the fact daily that our performance in research and development and science related activities lags behind that of all these world leaders. I agree it does in many different ways.
Spending comes to mind. It is true, sir, that we are spending significantly less, that is, in terms of a percentage of the Gross National Product, than do the United States, France, Germany, and the European Community, generally, particularly Japan. In fact, we are spending perhaps just a little over half
of what these countries are spending on science and technology. My socialist friends have cried that we should be spending more; massive amounts of new money should be contributed. The Liberals are saying that as well. The Liberals had 20 years to plan ahead.
Let me just draw you a profile of what we found when we arrived here three years ago, Mr. Speaker. We found absolutely no planning, no reading, no recognition of the trends that were clearly established at that point, the trends that will establish the role of a nation like Canada in the 21st Century. There was no forward planning. There were no resources set aside for science and technology or for research. More importantly, the apparatus of government was not arranged to respond to these new trends and priorities.
So what did we do? First, we had to plan ahead and develop a vision for Canada. We had to work with the other players, with the provinces, so we sat down with the provinces. It took us two years to develop a national policy for science and technology. It was not a policy that came out of this place, or out of some historic discussions in some back room. It was a policy signed by 10 of the provinces, the two territories and the national Government. It is a focus for Canada, a vision for Canada. It was signed in March of this year in Vancouver.
We have a national strategy called "Innovaction" which lays out a clear focus of where we want to go and what we must do to respond to the challenge. We established a Standing Committee of this House of Commons on Research, Science and Technology for the first time. We established a central coordinating agency to manage the $4.2 billion the federal Government spends annually on science and technology to ensure that we do not duplicate our effort, that it is properly co-ordinated so that we use our scarce resources to lever private sector activities.
In our international comparisons we found as well that the effort of the federal Government was not at all bad. It was quite respectable when one compares what the federal Government spends in Canada with what the U.S. Government spends in the United States, particularly when one considers that over three-quarters of the expenditures in the United States, for instance-and that holds true for France, although not so much for Japan-is spent on defence related research and development activities. So there is quite a profound difference. We do not spend that much money on defence. We have perhaps other priorities.
We did find that we have a lot of catching up to do. We have to mobilize our resources. First, we needed to know what we wanted to spend our additional resources on. We needed to reorganize the apparatus of Government to ensure that we have the proper advice. As you know, sir, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) appointed a council of the most prominent prestigious people in the country. It is a council which advises him personally on matters related to science and technology. That council has been meeting now for a year and is coming up with all kinds of interesting solutions and suggestions.
August 25, 1987

What have we done in the area of spending? My friend said this morning we have done nothing, that we are doing less now than we did when we came on stream. Let me put the record straight, as I did the other day. We are hearing the lament that we are not making any progress in finding new resources. Well, Sir, 1 made a comparison between the period since our mandate, the last three years, and the three years preceding our mandate. We have achieved an increase in spending in research and development and science related activities, that is the total national effort, including the private sector and universities. The provinces are spending very little; it is mainly the federal Government. In real dollars; that is, discounting inflation, we increased our effort by 21 per cent. That is very respectable. With the incentives we have put in place, and by our removing some of the obstacles, business has increased its effort by 23 per cent in real dollars.
The National Research Council had these drastic cuts. My friends will tell us every day we slashed our spending, but there has been a 23 per cent increase in allocation to the National Research Council in the last three years over the three years preceding.
Then we put in place provincial subagreements in order to get the provinces involved in this national thrust. There was an increase of 40 per cent in the worth of science and technology subagreements. That is very respectable in light of this other compelling priority of which we are not ashamed, and that is to bring our fiscal house into order and to quit mortgaging the future of the next 10 generations.
There is one other overriding and compelling urgency and obstacle that stands in the way of our objectives and that is the lack of a management regime, an investment climate and a regulatory environment within which the private sector would play its rightful role in the scheme of things. This, of course, is because of the antiquated patent laws and the antiquated ways we manage our intellectual capital under the Copyright Act and other such Acts. It is in that area where we are now moving as quickly as we can because we are not dealing only with pharmaceuticals, we are dealing with computer software as well.
We lose jobs every day because computer software companies cannot do research in Canada. When they are finished, they have to patent their findings in other countries. Until we reward people and permit them the right to keep some of the fruits of their labours, we will pot get research in the pharmaceutical industries.
We know what will happen when Bill C-22 comes into force because of some of the initiatives that have already taken place. Almost every week I am invited to attend press conferences at which major companies announce the establishment of labs in Canada, and particularly in the Montreal region which has become a centre for the pharmaceutical sector. There will be at least 3,000 jobs and $1.4 billion in new
Patent Act
investment. That is how to improve efforts in science and technology and R and D.
Try as we might, the federal Government, even if joined by the provinces, would not be able to respond to the challenges. That response requires the mobilization of our combined energies and resources. It requires the intellectual genius that resides in Canada. Every citizen must know what is happening in this new world and must be prepared for it. Every sector of the economy including traditional industries must become knowledge-intensive in planning and must use new technologies to improve efforts.
Our science and technology strategy is geared toward the revitalization of traditional industries including the forestry, mining, agricultural and fisheries sectors. Those are traditional industries which have been the basis of the prosperity we have enjoyed. The federal Government is playing a key role in important research in all these areas.
We must revitalize the regions that have become so dependent on primary resource industries. We must permit them to retain and improve their competitive postures in world markets. As Hon. Members know, commodity prices are under serious pressures as the technological revolution produces all kinds of substitutes for traditional materials with which we build our automobiles and homes. We must use technologies to stay on the cutting edge of technology. We must convert and add value to our resources and the refining of them.
Our national strategy on R and D and new technology is also designed to develop new technology-intensive industries. No longer will it be good enough for Canada to import 80 per cent of all the construction machinery and equipment that is used in the resource sectors. Entire sawmill systems are imported from Finland, Germany and the United States. However, we export 80 per cent of all the products of our aerospace industry. What a source of pride that is for all of us. We have ignored important opportunities we can now cash in on as we plan our new strategy in science and technology.
The challenges are great. The opportunities are unlimited. We cannot afford to allow a group of people who held prominent positions and served the country well in another age, but who are now sitting in the Senate, respectful as we are of this great institution, to deprive the present generation and future generations of Canadians of their place in the sun. We shall not stand for that.
We must decide by whose rules we want to play to achieve our place in the sun and to stay in the fast current that is sweeping mankind toward this new age. We on this side have made our decision. We will build on the great tradition of Canada. We will remobilize and rekindle the entrepreneurial spirit that made this country great in the first place. In order to do that, we have to play by the rules of the western world, of which we are an important part, and not by any other rules. We have no choice.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to see that the Prime Minister is still here. Before speaking about Bill C-22, I would like to challenge him to solve a problem. Bill C-22 is not a problem caused by the Senators. If the Prime Minister has the courage of his convictions, since he has said that he has no need for the support of the Opposition with his majority, let him table his Bill in this House and we shall debate it.
As for Bill C-22, it is not a matter of having a debate between the House of Commons and the Senate. What is sad in this whole debate, Mr. Speaker, is that if we look at today's demonstration-I have nothing against the demonstration; I went to meet those people-we find that they are all employees of the industry, and it is no surprise to learn that they were given a day off and sent on a luxury bus to Parliament Hill. I am not blaming those people for having accepted to make this trip to save their jobs.
The next thing we shall hear in this fight about patent protection, is that, next week, the generic companies will put up some money, close up shop and give a day off to their employees so that they can come here in luxury buses and demonstrate on the Hill.
In fact, this is a job war between two types of companies, the multinationals and the others, and if the latter had the opportunity to become multinationals, they would behave just like the first. However, what we have to remember as Parliamentarians and representatives of the Canadian people, is what the consequences will be for Canadian men and women.
In this case, we are talking about the health of individuals. Everyone in Canada supports research, not only scientific research, but all kinds of research. If we want to promote research, instead of financing the Western banks when they go bankrupt, instead of giving money to the rich, we should put back some money in university research, create jobs and innovate to cure the sick and give them back their health.
However, the Conservative Government says: No, here is what we are going to do, the multinationals have asked for a ten year protection, and we are going to give in to blackmail and do as they wish. We, Liberals, refuse to do so. This is not how we operate. Such a simple concept as saying that it would be better to increase taxes on everything to create jobs, something as stupid as saying ... A PC Member may rise and say: Well, since jobs are being lost in the funeral home industry, we are going to encourage euthanasia to create jobs. Come on! As if this was a principle upon which we could play with people's health, Mr. Speaker.
Instead of stubbornly maintaining its position or organizing a demonstration ... I referred to the representatives of multinationals. These people know what bargaining is all about. They should say: What is this all about? Now, there is no protection. While I am talking, the people of the Conservative Opposition could protect jobs, they want us to cry out. .. When you abolished the quotas to protect jobs in the footwear industry, was it because they were not university people? Are you going to protect these jobs because they are university people? They are certainly well paid. But when you were asked to protect the jobs of the men and women working in the Quebec footwear and textile industries, either in the Eastern Townships or in some Ontario regions represented by Conservative Members, you said: No way. We are negotiating free trade with the Americans.
August 25, 1987

But now, there are big American guys with pockets full of dollars who say that you have to protect the brains. But whose brains? This depends on the years you have spent in school.
Mr. Speaker, I suggest that we, as Members of the Liberal Party, have a position. It is my friend the Hon. Member for Saint-Michel who was the first to open the debate on this issue. Also, the previous Liberal Government had requested an independent inquiry by specialists who claimed that, to protect research, security, create jobs and prevent undue increases in the prices of medicine, a four-year protection was enough. All additional years on top of the first four were what is called "gravy", additional money in the pockets of multinationals.
I am not here to blame multinationals, for the heads of such corporations are sincere. They say: Claude, I have that much money to invest. But we remember that not so long ago, some oil multinationals in Western Canada told this Conservative Government: If you change the energy policy, we are going to invest so much money. Everybody was honest and sincere at the time. Then suddenly the oil crisis occurred and they said: Sorry, 1 just cannot.
Right now there is nothing in the legislation as put forward by this Tory Government that guarantees jobs to Montrealers, of which I am one. And I know very well the new jobs that will be created will not necessarily be for people in my constituency of Sainte-Marie. But I am here to defend the interests of the people in Sainte-Marie, and if 1 bow to the multinational corporations blackmail, or on the other hand if I yield too much to generic companies, I will not protect consumers in my constituency of Montreal-Sainte-Marie and elsewhere in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister who was supposed to be a top-notch mediator could have taken this opportunity to prove his talent, because since the beginning, almost three years now, it has been failure and catastrophe. Mediator my foot, the outcome was nil. But it is my feeling and my deep conviction that in order to protect the interests of consumers, which comes first, and when we refer to consumers we are referring to people who buy, not candies but drugs because they have some ailment. This is a matter of survival. I know this is not a great concern of Conservative Members, because they even slapped a 12 per cent tax on drugs, even on syringes used by people with diabetes in order to survive.
Certainly we must have compassion. It is of vital importance to ensure that those people can afford to buy drugs. Some will suggest this is a matter for provincial governments. But who pays for Provincial Governments, who pays for employer-employee health insurance? The middle income taxpayer always gets clobbered. Three million Canadians are not protected by any form of insurance. Today, 1 beg the Prime Minister to sit down with the multinationals and say: Just one minute! You had your way with me once when I was President
Patent Act
of Iron Ore. You had me close down the place and tip-toe out of the picture, but this time I won't be had.
In the bill-you're asking for 10 years; at present you have nothing, so let's opt for a middle course. Let's make a deal, let's negotiate. We'll go for five years in the bill. And five years down the road we will review the impact on consumers, the impact in terms of profitability and job creation. At that time and given that experience, we will be in a position to reconsider our decision and either renew for another five years, increase the protection to seven years or decrease it to three years. It seems logical to me and probably to managers of corporations and I even invite my friend Robert Bourassa, from Quebec. I know for a fact that Ti-Louis Laberge does not sleep around with the multinationals just to generate employment, and neither do Mr. Larose and Jean Dore, the Mayor of Montreal. I know these people well enough to know that they want to protect employment, yes, but not if it means choking to death those who suffer from illness in Quebec. That is how I feel and I invite the Conservative Members, who are quick to jump on the bandwagon as we remember from the old age security de-indexation saga. These fellows had really found their way to the heart of all senior citizens. I recall that the Hon. Member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mrs. Bertrand) had said at the time that the Government was not bound by its promises. Not telling the truth to just about anybody was of no great consequence. But today, 79 percent of the population does not trust that Prime Minister any more.
There is something else I want to say. The Senate has a role to play in that matter. There is no doubt in my mind right now that the Senate accomplished a part of the job they are assigned under the Constitution. The Conservative Government is the one to blame. The Prime Minister has been making statements in every part of the country. He has bragged in Alberta, he has bragged in Quebec: "We will abolish the Senate, we will do such and such a thing to the Senate." Back here, he behaves like a lamb and does nothing. One day, he talks of abolishing the Senate. But what are we to make of a Prime Minister who says the Senate is an undemocratic institution? His chief negotiator on constitutional affairs is a senator. Because nobody was brilliant and competent enough in the Conservative caucus for that job, the Prime Minister had to seek somebody from an undemocratic body. When one does not believe in an institution, one does not appoint to it friends such as Bazin and others connected with the whole Oerlikon affair. How can we explain this and how can the people trust a Prime Minister who does not speak clearly and frankly? That is why I invite those Members over there who are reasonable to bring the Prime Minister to his senses.
1 think a large majority of Quebecers are for it. I do not want to be dishonest, to play the same game as the Prime Minister and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and try to make believe all Quebecers are in favour.
I could give you a whole list of people and organizations on record as being squarely and totally against Bill C-22, like the NDP. I do not share that view. I can take my responsabilities.

August 25, 1987

However, you cannot, as the Conservatives claim, make people believe that all associations of senior citizens or consumers are for that Bill. It is not so. If Hon. Members do not lie, they are poorly informed. There are people who totally disagree. But the vast majority-I was at the Economic Summit in Montreal, but neither the Hon. Member for Beauce (M. Bernier) nor the Hon. Members from Alberta were there. At this Summit were members of municipal governments, union representatives, senior citizens that I know very well, and officials of the provincial government. In principle, people for Metropolitan Montreal, and I support them, are for job creation, for protection of job creation.
But job creation in Montreal, Mr. Speaker, is called Space Agency. We do not necessarily want jobs immediately if it means higher prices for those who are sick. There are other actions that the Government should have taken to create jobs in the Montreal area. The situation has been going on for three years: Montreal East is in ruins, the shipyards are desperate. The Government wakes up suddenly. As a Montrealer, I cannot accept it for the good of the whole population of Montreal-Sainte-Marie, I cannot support the Conservative Party and allow that 10 year protection.
All the experts have clearly shown that a five-year protection for patents is more than enough for the companies to recover their investment. Second, in spite of all that has been said and with the best will in the world, and I believe that these people do want to invest, there is no guarantee that they will. We all remember the promises made by the Conservatives. Who can still believe the Prime Minister?
We all recall the de-indexation of old age security pensions. The Prime Minister had sworn that he would re-establish full indexation of old age security pensions, and he did the exact opposite. The same happened for family allowances. A report of this Government stated that the changes to the family support programs such as family allowances and the child tax credit would not be used to reduce the deficit. It was written in black and white. We had the word of the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Once more, we were misled. The Minister of Finance took nearly $2 billion from the family support programs to reduce the deficit. Then, there was the case of the banks which went bankrupt.
Even more recently, the Government has talked about imposing a tax on food, that is on bread, milk and butter. As I said earlier, according to the polls, 71 per cent of Canadians are against this idea. Within a very short time this summer, 25,000 people throughout Quebec and Canada signed a petition asking the Government to abandon this idea. Even the members of the Conservative caucus, not because they believe in this, but because they know that the public has put pressure on them to do so, have asked the Prime Minister to give up this idea.
Once again, we see the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) dragging his feet, unable to state clearly his options and unwilling once more to take action. But I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the national petition and awareness campaign is not over yet as far as we are concerned. If the Prime Minister had clearly stated today his opposition, we would have ended that campaign but now, we are going to keep it up throughout Canada.
And as I travel all across the main regions of Montreal to speak about patent and job protection, I can see that it is not the people who are complaining and are asking for that protection. Of course and it is quite understandable that those company owners should ask for that protection. What I dislike in this debate is the fact that-and it is normal in the case of competitors of that company that they too should ask for a lesser protection-one of them is trying to hoodwink us but I was not born yesterday and I know that for those people, money is the bottom line-and it goes for both sides, and the only thing they are interested in.
But for us, as parliamentarians, our role is not to make a choice between those companies. I agree that with their free market philosophy this is how the Conservatives would put it. I would like the Conservative members who will later comment and ask questions to tell us why in the regions of Quebec, Beauce, the Eastern Townships or the South shore, they did not fight to maintain jobs and the protected quotas in the shoe industry? Why didn't they fight for and protect the interests of their constituents who were asking for it? Why are the Conservatives crawling before the multinational drug companies and giving them that ten year protection?
We know perfectly well that drug prices will go up because the Government would not otherwise pay back several million dollars to provincial governments. In fact, where there is a provincial drug plan the provincial or the federal Government will have to raise taxes and taxpayers will end up footing the bill anyway.
Mr. Speaker, I did not hear many Conservative Members from the Montreal area-in fact those who still behave themselves have kept pretty quiet and the rest are involved in scandals. I wonder how many of them have not yet been dragged in some shaddy deal?
I would like the Hon. Member for Beauce (Mr. Bernier) to tell me, for instance, how many senior citizens in his area feel that as in the case of the proposal to de-index old age security pensions, government members wanted to make us believe that senior citizens were for it. But when the Prime Minister backed down, everybody admitted to be against it . Well, I am suspicious of anyone who on two or three occasions has already, unintentionally, perhaps because of poor judgment, misled the Canadian people. Following public meetings and demonstrations, finally, the Government had to recognize that the Official Opposition was right.
August 25, 1987

Next week, on September 4, this Government will celebrate its third anniversary. 1 realize that those three years have been passing too fast for those in power. I also realize that those three years have been disastrous. But they have been particularly bad for the people.
If the university report is any indication, low and middle income families are the people who have been despicably attacked and deprived of a sizable portion of their purchasing power. This Bill as it is now drafted, Mr. Speaker, would strike another hard blow at these people, again the elderly and middle income families.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would point out that when the provincial Government of Quebec pays for drugs, most of the time the list of drugs covered includes only generic products. This is something the Conservative Members should keep in mind.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart) poses as the champion of the poor, yet now that we want to promote a sector of activities where wages are high, where we seek to push them higher still, the Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie keeps saying that we are working against poor people. Mr. Speaker, Mr. Bourassa, the Premier of Quebec and Quebec's Opposition Party voted a unanimous resolution in Quebec's National Assembly on Bill C-22. The Hon. Member said earlier that Mr. Bourassa was his friend. That may be true, but the feeling may not be mutual.
Mr. Speaker, I just don't understand those Liberal and NDP Members who are trying to defend the poor and at the same time prevent jobs from being created. I don't know what they can be thinking of. Maybe they think jobs and money grow on trees. As far as I know, jobs and money come from the private sector. They keep telling us we are helping the multinationals. That is not true. We are helping people, men and women, to find jobs in areas where they can earn a decent salary, a very decent salary, instead of trying to find jobs for the poor. I think Canada is a country where there is more to do than just draw water and tighten screws on the assembly line. Canada also has an educated labour force that is capable of doing research and developrhent. That is what we are trying to promote, and that is how this country is going to get rid of part of the poverty that exists today. We have to look at the fundamentals instead of just skimming the surface and trying to use the poor as a way to criticize the Government. We want to raise the standard of living of everyone in this country.
The Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie is not addressing these fundamental issues honestly. He refuses to acknowledge that we as a Government are acting in good faith by promoting well-paying jobs. Just because we want to help people in Canada get better salaries, that does not mean we are playing favourites with the private sector and the multinationals. I think it is better to have research done in Canada than in the United States or Europe.
Patent Act
Well, in the area of medicinal drugs, the competition is international, if we want to maintain our competitive position and create jobs in this country, we must carry out research here. We should not abandon all this research to other nations. That is what the Liberal Party did some ten years ago. It allowed all investors, inventors and researchers to move to the United States or elsewhere. As the Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux) reminded us this morning, when the Liberals adopted this legislation about ten years ago, they completely cleaned out the buildings in Montreal West, buildings which have remained completely empty ever since. Well, they are now caught at their own game. Of course, we are defending ourselves on this level. Well, Mr. Speaker, I thank you very much and I ask the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte Marie to be honest and to explain to the Canadian and Quebec people why he is so anxious to keep only small jobs in Quebec. He should be proud to say that at last in Quebec our people are going to get involved in advanced technology and earn reasonable salaries, thereby making it possible for the Quebec economy to function better.

speechtext:
