speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say that the comments of my hon. friend with respect to the Senate are fascinating. Logically, I expect that there will be no further appointments to this devastating, undemocratic, difficult and unacceptable body in the future. I am sure the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) will be deeply disappointed. I am sure that the Prime Minister's friends will be even more deeply disappointed. I am interested to hear this strong position put by the Hon. Member.
The question of the Senate is very much a red herring as we carry forward this debate. The reality is that the Senate has typically, throughout our parliamentary history, occasionally brought back amendments to the House of Commons for us to consider. We have accepted amendments in some cases, such as in the case of transport deregulation Bills earlier last week. Of course, the Government accepted those amendments from the Senate without any of these diatribes against the right of the Senate to operate within our present constitutional framework.
I say to the Government, as it starts to play with fire on this issue, that there is a serious possibility that it will get itself into constitutional problems from which it will be very difficult to extricate itself. It is the Government's choice to make this debate about a piece of legislation which is, itself, most
August 25, 1987

devastating for most Canadians, a debate about the constitutionality of the Senate. I believe it is playing with fire and will live to regret it.
With that as a prelude, as trade critic for our Party, I want to say a few words about the connection between this Bill and the free trade negotiations which are taking place. First, let me say that it is quite clear that the pressure which started from the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association of Canada began well before the election of the Government. For instance, I have a copy of a detailed study on pressure groups and the federal Government, looking at the case of pharmaceutical lobbies and compulsory licensing. It is written by Mario Iacobacci. He makes it quite clear in this study that the previous Government faced a very strong lobby from the PMAC. That strong lobby has continued and we have seen more manifestations of it today.
It is interesting to note that the pressure being applied by the multinational drug companies not only took the form of pressure on Members of Parliament and cabinet Ministers through the PMAC, but took the form of pressure through the United States trade representative, William Brock at that time.
For instance, one source quoted in this study indicates:
Brock's influence on this issue has been fairly strong. When it was raised at the recent Brock-Kelleher meeting, it was named as the first of three items on the agenda in terms of importance.
Let me reiterate that this pressure started well before this Government came into office. There is a remarkable quotation from the present head lobbyist for the PMAC, Judy Erola, who at that time was a member of the Liberal Cabinet. She indicated the following:
When I came in it was a foregone conclusion that there would be changes to the Patent Act... If I had been in at the beginning I would not have had (compulsory licensing) reviewed. I would have looked at tax incentives ... If 1 had been Minister before, I would not have entertained any changes to the Patent Act, but the can of worms had already been opened.
As the author of the study goes on to say:
This exceptionally candid statement attests to the very important constraints that prevented at least this Minister, if not others, from dealing with the compulsory licensing issue in the way she deemed most appropriate.
It is important to recognize as well that this pressure from the United States to amend our drug patent laws has continued and has strengthened as the free trade negotiations have become part of the economic agenda of this country. For instance, if we look at the declaration from the Quebec summit of the Prime Minister and the President of the United States in March, 1985, there was agreement reached at that point on "co-operation to protect intellectual property rights from trade and counterfeit goods and other abuses of copyright and patent law".
In briefings which took place at that time, it was indicated that pharmaceuticals were one key part of what was being discussed in that particular item of the Quebec summit declaration.
Patent Act
Just as recently as this past weekend, we have had precisely the same kinds of indications in the press that make it quite clear that the United States is very interested in what happens to Bill C-22 and has tied that interest to what it is likely to do with respect to free trade negotiations. I quote from a story from The Globe and Mail which states: "Demonstrating resolve on C-22 will become important two months from now if the Canada-U.S. free trade negotiators come up with a tentative pact, which both Governments will then have to sell politically at home". The source for this article is then quoted as saying: "The White House isn't going to expend a lot of its political capital with Congress to sell a trade deal with Canada if we don't show we can pass a Bill like C-22 with our big majority". That very strongly suggests that what we have here in front of us is an example of quid pro quo.
We have a Government which prior to the fact is making commitments to the United States that it will carry out changes to our Patent Act in order to establish not what the recommendations of the detailed reports suggested but instead a 10-year monopoly on drug patents. In short, it will be 10 years in which drug companies, mainly from the United States but also from other countries as well-and I agree with the Hon. Member from Lachine on that point-will have the freedom to bring forward price changes which they can justify to a price review board. This will permit them to increase very, very significantly, I am certain, their profits and therefore the prices which Canadians have to pay, whether they pay them through taxes, medical care premiums or direct payments at the drugstore. That type of quid pro quo, that type of sell-out of our country, is simply not acceptable to this Party. It is something which we have fought throughout this debate from the moment it was introduced in the House until now. We will continue to fight it regardless of the fact that the amendments which happen to be the subject of discussion at the moment are from the Senate.
It is important to make several additional points in order to add to this sense of sell-out on the part of our Government. First, it is important to say that we have in front of us a Bill which does nothing to establish a monitoring agency which will see to it that the drug companies come through with the commitments which they have been announcing with such fanfare across the land. This includes companies which have made signed commitments, such as Firestone of the United States in the case of Hamilton, and which have backed off those commitments. What can we expect when we not only have nothing in the Bill in the way of commitments but we have nothing in it in the way of attempts to monitor the commitments which have supposedly been made?
Second, we have to look very hard at the question of jobs as suggested by the Minister and as suggested by the pharmaceutical companies themselves. In fact there have been detailed examinations of these jobs, the supposed 300,000 high-tech jobs which will be provided by this legislation. There

August 25, 1987
Patent Act
are indications that in fact only 1,148 of those jobs will be jobs in the professional category in the industry itself. Another 652 will be classified as technical. One would expect that these would be reasonable jobs, but they are not high-tech jobs. Finally, 620 jobs turn out to be cleaning jobs, jobs for animal keepers, statisticians, clerks, et cetera. So much for the 3,000 jobs which have been promised by the industry.
So we do not really have a commitment which holds any water in terms of providing any faith to be placed in these companies by the Government or by the Canadian people. This Bill which has been with us for a long time makes me think of the fact that prior to its introduction Canada existed as a country which was a leader in the industrialized world. It was not the only country taking such a lead. There are other countries, such as Italy, whose pharmaceutical patent laws are much looser than those of this country. We were taking a lead to see to it that in an industry dominated by multinational companies it would be possible to give a fair break to the consumer and the taxpayer. That lead was an important example to the rest of the world with respect to what could be done. It could still provide an important example to the rest of the world of what could be done if we permitted compulsory licensing to continue with the same freedom which we have permitted in the past.
Members forget that there were repeated attempts made to deal with drug prices before 1969. It proved impossible to bring those prices down. But with the legislation which was passed to provide for compulsory licensing it proved possible to bring prices down for the consumer and to give to Canadian producers a chance to enter the drug industry despite the patent conditions held by the multinational drug companies.
1 consider it a great shame that with this piece of legislation Canada is moving from being a leader, a leader attempting to obtain both research and lower prices for consumers, to being a follower, a follower of the United States. We are becoming followers of the United States in the context of an abject attempt to reach a free trade agreement, but also a follower in the sense of simply accepting what the United States has done in terms of patent legislation affecting drugs.
If it takes the Senate to force us to have another look at this Bill, this is the one occasion, and I hope it is the single occasion in my life, in which 1 have to offer praise to the Senate. I think that we have received a set of improvements from the Senate. Frankly, it is not a set of improvements which are exactly what I would like to see, but at least it is an approach which is better than the one taken by the Government.
I urge the Flouse to take the Bill to defeat what the Conservative Government is attempting to do, and to give back to Canada a sense of leadership, independence, and freedom from pressure from the United States.

I mentioned that Bill C-22 is good for Alberta companies. I would like to talk about three Alberta-based companies and to outline benefits they will see if Bill C-22 is passed.
Biomira Inc. is an Edmonton company which spends $3 million per year on the research and development of a cancer vaccine. Its President, Gordon Politeski, knows that his company will benefit. If this Bill is passed, he plans to expand his research program, but if it is not passed, he is seriously considering relocating to the United States or another country which grants the patent protection which pharmaceutical research deserves.
Chembio-Med is 100 per cent-owned by the University of Alberta and has 50 employees. It is expected to grow quickly if the Bill is passed. Synphar Pharmaceuticals is a new company which has 20 employees. It hopes to grow to 250 by 1990. I mention these companies because they will be hiring at the scientist and researcher levels. These are levels where there were previously few opportunities. All three firms rely on the passage of Bill C-22 to expand.
There will be new companies as well. The Calgary Research and Development Authority, a group which is sponsored by the City of Calgary, the Chamber of Commerce and the University of Calgary, was formed to foster research and a research-based technology industry in that city. Mr. Croft, the President of that organization, explained to the legislative committee studying this Bill that biological and genetic research now being developed at the University of Alberta and the University of Calgary could provide the basis for a new high-tech sector. This could only occur after the system of allowing companies to copy new pharmaceuticals is changed.
I would like to refer to Mr. Croft again because one of his statements summarized the difficulties faced by Alberta companies. He argued that the inhibiting nature of compulsory licensing is demonstrated by the absence in Alberta of small pharmaceutical research firms, even though the province has become an emerging centre of other high-tech firms.

The Calgary Herald explained that Alberta hospitals, universities and research centres stand to gain $100 million in private grants for drug research in the next 10 years if this Bill is passed. Those are private grants, not government money. That is a tenfold increase over what is now being spent.
We can see the effect in how well Alberta universities can compete. The University of Calgary's researchers have a proud list of pharmacological projects, including research into anticancer drugs such as Interferon and new anti-diabetic agents.
Passage of Bill C-22 will be good for Alberta health care as it will be good for health care across the country. All Members of this House know the Bill does not affect drugs currently on the market. It applies only to drugs which may be invented in the future. I therefore find it reprehensible that Members of this House who know better are attempting to use scare tactics on senior citizens and others by suggesting that somehow this Bill will increase the cost of drugs they use. That is totally false. Any suggestion like that is an attempt to mislead the public. This Bill seeks to create an environment where we can increase scientific research and development in drugs and health care and build an industry to produce and sell those drugs.
It is useful to compare the original Bill and the Senate version with respect to jobs and cost to consumers. I know the Consumers' Association of Canada has not supported this Bill. I spoke to the President of that association, one of my constituents, earlier today. However, I would like to point out that the original Bill will result in a $1.4 billion investment in new research and 3,000 jobs. The Senate's royalty scheme would produce a fund of between $140 million and $225 million. Similarly, over 10 years, according to the Eastman report, the cost to consumers would be in the neighbourhood of $700 million to $1.1 billion. The Senate proposal does not include a drug prices review board. We can only conclude that the Senate's proposals are far more detrimental to the consumer than the Government's legislation and they have nowhere near the economic benefits of the original Bill.
This Bill is not about drugs, it is about jobs. We can allow research and development to be done in the U.S., Japan and Europe and buy the products they produce, or we can develop our own industry. This Bill is also about democracy and whether or not an unelected institution can thwart the will of elected representatives.

UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-INQUIRY WHY ELDERLY WORKER WITH COLLECTIVE PENSION PLAN IS PENALIZED- INQUIRY WHY THERE ARE TWO CLASSES OF ELDERLY WORKERS IN CANADA-INQUIRY WHY CERTAIN CATEGORY OF ELDERLY WORKERS IS PENALIZED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after a debate which clearly showed once more the indifference and lack of concern of this Conservative Government for the Canadian people, I would like to come back to a question which I asked the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) about the unemployment insurance benefits of older workers.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that it is important to remind the Members of this House and those Canadians who are now listening to us in their homes that, in the past, when an older worker lost his job, accepted early retirement to protect the jobs of younger workers and continued looking for work even though he received benefits from the pension plan to which he had contributed, he was also entitled to unemployment insurance benefits. Unfortunately, in January 1985, this

August 25, 1987
Adjournment Debate
Conservative Government decided to put an end to this practice, and without informing those who had applied for unemployment insurance benefits after taking an early retirement, the Government cut off their benefits.
After a hard fight of 17 or 18 months and with the support of thousands of older workers in the regions of Quebec City, Sherbrooke, Abitibi, Rouyn-Noranda, the North Shore, Montreal, and especially the Montreal-Sainte-Marie constituency, we were able to make the Government go back on its decision and reverse its position, just as we had done in the case of the partial de-indexation of old age security pensions
As of now, 46,000 older workers in Canada have been reimbursed the unemployment insurance benefits to which they were entitled and received an average of $10,000 each.
Unfortunately, and in this case, I asked my question to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard), because of the silence and indifference of the Conservative and New Democrat Members who have done nothing about this issue, we have to continue our representations because there are 2,500 other workers in Canada who lost their jobs before January 5, 1986, and had accepted to take early retirement under the rules which applied at the time.
But unfortunately these people were known to have left their employers on December 31, 1985. New Year's is a holiday and the offices of employment centres are closed, so the Government does not want to do them justice quite simply because the men and women who went to see the Canada Manpower Centre staff to apply for unemployment insurance benefits were told by the officials: No, you are not eligible right now. Come back in three weeks or a month because you just got your severance pay. So they did come back, but today the Government refuses to reimburse them.
This is what I would like to know from the Member or the Parliamentary Secretary who will be answering my question: On the basis of what social justice principle does this Conservative Government maintain two classes of older workers? We have an older worker who has set aside part of his wages and transferred that part to an employer pension plan, and we have another older worker in another company who has saved up part of his income to contribute to a Registered Retirement Savings Plan. The result is that the latter is entitled to draw full unemployment insurance benefits, even if he is receiving $400 or $500 per week from his RRSP. Unfortunately for Canadians listening to us now who opted for early retirement, when they were hired, like our public servants and our military, they had to pay unemployment insurance benefits and contribute to an employer pension plan.
But when these people lose their jobs, and there are hundreds and thousands of people losing their jobs in the regions, they go to the Unemployment Insurance Office and they are told: No. The Mulroney Government will not give you your unemployment insurance benefits. The Conservative Government and Conservative Members say: No, we don't
trust your word, we don't believe you. Go get another job. If you do find another job and you lose it, then you will be eligible. That is outrageous! It is completely outrageous, Mr. Speaker, to treat a worker like this.
Mr. Speaker, I wish the Minister's Parliamentary Secretary would tell us why, on the basis of what kind of social justice, his Government is proceeding in this way. How can Conservative Members meet older workers and still talk to them without shame? And this decision does not apply just to today's older workers, it applies to all workers.
Today, Conservative Members were pulling out all the emotional stops to save jobs, Mr. Speaker, but I think it is time justice were done.
Mr. Speaker, you are telling me my time has expired. I hope the Parliamentary Secretary has good news-not for me but for thousands of older workers who are awaiting the Government's decision. I hope he says his Government will reimburse all older workers and eliminate this discriminatory treatment of our workers.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-INQUIRY WHY ELDERLY WORKER WITH COLLECTIVE PENSION PLAN IS PENALIZED- INQUIRY WHY THERE ARE TWO CLASSES OF ELDERLY WORKERS IN CANADA-INQUIRY WHY CERTAIN CATEGORY OF ELDERLY WORKERS IS PENALIZED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to respond to the question raised by the Hon. Member on March 31 concerning unemployment insurance and pensions.
Pension agreements constitute an essential part of an employee's earning package. It is the Government's view that pension income is paid as compensation when regular earnings are no longer forthcoming and that persons who have retired from the labour market should not look to unemployment insurance as a supplementary source of income in retirement.
The unemployment insurance regulations regarding the treatment of pension income were introduced on January 5, 1986. However, as the Hon. Member will recall, on December 5, 1986, the Government announced its intention to amend the regulations. The Bill which the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) recently introduced in the House will enable persons in receipt of pension income to requalify for full unemployment insurance benefits if they take a job after their retirement and they work long enough to qualify for unemployment insurance benefits.
Furthermore, the Minister of Employment and Immigration indicated to the House on March 18 that persons who had applied for unemployment insurance prior to January 5, 1986-those people who applied under the previous rules-will have their entitlement to unemployment insurance benefits determined under the previous rules. It should therefore be obvious that the Government has bent over backwards to ensure that persons taking early retirement are treated equitably and fairly.
August 25, 1987

The Eton. Member implies that there is no fundamental difference between an employer-sponsored pension plan and a regular Registered Retirement Savings Plan. However, this simply is not correct. Pension plans are a term and condition of employment generally requiring contributions by both employer and employee to finance future pensions. Thus, they take the form of deferred employment earnings.
A Retirement Savings Plan, on the other hand, is based predominantly on a voluntary, individual savings decision. It is only one among many ways that an individual may accumulate savings.
I want to conclude by affirming the Government's resolve to treat all persons, including older workers, equitably and fairly under the unemployment insurance system while, at the same time, reinforcing the fundamental role of unemployment insurance as a scheme for temporarily replacing lost employment income.

subtopic: REFUGEES-REPORTS OF POSSIBLE ARRIVAL OF TAMILS FROM GERMANY
REFUGEES-REPORTS OF POSSIBLE ARRIVAL OF TAMILS FROM GERMANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 10 I asked the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) what the Government planned to do to prevent further abuse of our immigration and refugee policies. My question was in response to a large influx of Central Americans coming across our Canadian border from the United States and also because of rumours that possibly more Tamils would land on our shores.
The Minister replied that he would introduce legislation to clear up the problem and he followed through with his plan. Shortly after our interaction in this House, he announced a series of very responsible administrative changes to the refugee claims system. These revisions increased our ability to help genuine refugees while deterring system abuse.
At that time, the blanket policy on admissions and nondeportation which applied to certain countries was cancelled. As well, people coming from those countries whose citizens required visas to visit Canada were required to have transit visas if they were travelling through Canada en route to another destination. I was encouraged by these measures but continued to press for legislation to meet the increasing number of claimants.
As we all know, people claiming refugee status landed on our shores in July. The Immigration Act of 1976 stated that anyone in Canada, whether here legally or illegally, be given the right to a determination of their claim by the Minister, and a redetermination before the Immigration Appeal Board of any claim rejected by the Minister.
The Ministers of Immigration were bound by law to allow these people to stay in Canada. Cries of "Ship them back" were absolutely out of the question. Canada is a law-abiding country.
Adjournment Debate
Just two months before this, Bill C-55, amendments to the Immigration Act of 1976, had been introduced. The Opposition Parties strongly opposed the Bill, saying that it was too tough. I agree that it is tough, but it is fair. Even more important, it is necessary.
My constituency office in Fraser Valley East was inundated with calls and letters from Canadians who feel that those aboard the boat were jumping the queue, making it even more difficult for legitimate refugees to be processed through the legal channels. They asked me to pass on the message that Bill C-55 must be passed, and I did so gladly.
As a sovereign country, Canada must have the right to decide who comes into our country. Our laws must be strong enough to prevent further abuse. Too many people are now claiming entry who are not genuine refugees. I am satisfied that Bill C-55 and the recent legislation, Bill C-84, the deterrents and detention Bill, will make it clear to all people that Canada cannot and will not permit this abuse to continue. We will stop bogus refugees.
As a result of the request of our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to the Speaker of the House that Parliament be recalled, Bill C-55 and Bill C-84 have been read a second time and referred to legislative committees for examination. 1 trust that my hon. colleagues on both sides of the House will recognize the importance of these two pieces of legislation and will not attempt tactics to slow down the process. We have to rationalize our law toward refugees as soon as possible.
Bill C-55 remains committed to genuine refugees in need of our protection by establishing an independent body, the Immigration and Refugee Board. Cases will not be referred to this board when claimants are returnable to a safe third country, or if they fail to establish a well founded fear of persecution by not providing sufficient support of their claim, or if there are significant doubts as to the credibility of the evidence supporting their claims for this status.
The deterrents and detention Bill introduced this summer will substantially increase the penalties for traffickers of human cargo to a 10-year jail sentence and $500,000 fines. It will also impose heavier fines and penalties on transportation companies that bring undocumented people to Canada. The vast majority of improperly documented persons do not come in by the boatload, but actually by Canadian ports of entry on scheduled carriers. This means that we will have one law and this law will apply to all groups who overstep the rules. We cannot have two sets of laws for one situation.
As we have often heard, many who arrive illegally do not have any documentation. The deterrents Bill will require claimants to remain in detention for up to 21 days rather than seven if they do not possess proper documentation. If necessary, additional detention can be required until identity is proven. Since many Canadians expressed serious concerns about the background of certain refugees, this Bill will give the Government the power to remove people who pose a criminal or security threat to Canada.

August 25, 1987
Adjournment Debate
I believe that these two pieces of legislation, Bill C-55 and Bill C-84, are absolutely essential and are supported by the majority of Canadians. It is imperative that we protect bona fide refugees. We must tell the world that Canada will continue to open her arms to real refugees but we will not allow our laws to be abused or thwarted, nor will we let our record of humanitarianism become a laughing matter.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bud Bradley (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: REFUGEES-REPORTS OF POSSIBLE ARRIVAL OF TAMILS FROM GERMANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to expand upon the reply given by the Hon. Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) to the Hon. Member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Belsher) on February 10, 1987. I thank him for his comments on a subject that I know he holds very dear to his heart and on which he has worked very hard in our caucus.
In reply to the Hon. Member's question as to what we are doing to prevent further abuse of our immigration and refugee policies, I would draw the Member's attention to our recent efforts in this respect.
On February 20, 1987, this Government instituted control measures to stem the flow of illegal migrants posing as genuine refugees coming to Canada. These measures covered three primary areas. First, the cancellation of the existing blanket policy of admission or non-deportation of nationals of certain countries, which meant that all claimants, regardless of their country of origin, were treated in the same way. Second, the enforcement of existing provisions under the Immigration Act allowing us to better control the flow of refugee claimants from the United States. Pursuant to this measure, claimants remain temporarily in the United States until immigration hearings can take place. Third, the imposition of transit visas to stop illegal migrants from using the short stopover in Canada to claim refugee status.
These control measures, designed to discourage the arrival of economic migrants posing as genuine refugees, have been successful in that the number of arrivals has dropped dramatically. There were over 4,200 potential refugee claimants who appeared at Canada's ports of entry in February. This number was reduced to over 1,700 in March and stabilized at just over 1,600 in July, 1987.
The Government has also gone on to introduce two important pieces of legislation, Bills C-55 and C-84, which are presently in the committee stage, and to which the Hon. Member has alluded. His knowledge possibly exceeds mine in that area.
Bill C-55 establishes a new refugee determination system, indeed, a fair and efficient system which will result in the speedy resolution of refugee claims. This new Bill replaces the current eight-step process by a three-step system which will put an end to long delays and uncertainty for genuine refugees while speedily removing rejected claimants.
More recently the Government tabled Bill C-84 which embodies firmer deterrent measures designed to dovetail with Bill C-55 to provide immediate protection from abuse. The Bill strikes out the sources of the abuse by substantially increasing penalties for smugglers and strengthening security enforcement. Persons who arrive without proper documentation will be detained until their identities can be established; transportation companies carrying undocumented persons will be more heavily fined; and persons posing criminal and security threats will be swiftly removed.
With these measures we can better manage our borders, and deter abuse. We renew our abiding commitment that genuine refugees will continue to be welcomed in Canada.

subtopic: CORPORATE AFFAIRS-HIGH INTEREST RATES CHARGED TO CREDIT CARD USERS-INTERVENTION BY ILLINOIS STATE TREASURER
CORPORATE AFFAIRS-HIGH INTEREST RATES CHARGED TO CREDIT CARD USERS-INTERVENTION BY ILLINOIS STATE TREASURER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to try to get the Government to act on the rip-off which major banks, retail companies and energy companies are forcing on hundreds of thousands of Canadians, mostly, or almost all of whom are in low or middle-income brackets.
The interest rate on unpaid balances of credit card users charged by the banks which operate Mastercard and Visa, those who operate the major retail chains such as Eaton's, The Bay and Sears, and the gasoline companies, vary from 16.5 per cent to 28.8 per cent. On top of that many of these institutions have instituted a user-fee of $1 per month or a transaction fee of 25 cents per transaction.
These rates came into effect in the early 1980s when the prime rate set by the Bank of Canada was almost twice as high as it is today. At that time I suppose it was necessary for these companies issuing credit cards to set their rates in the 20 per cent or more range, which is what they did. The prime rate set by the Bank of Canada, the rates which banks charge and the rates which they pay to depositors have come down substantially. Yet the banks and the other organizations such as retail chains and energy companies have stubbornly refused to bring down their interest rates.
It took repeated speeches, repeated questions, an inquiry by the Finance Committee of the House of Commons, as well as a threat by the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) before the banks which operate the major credit card groups such as Mastercard and Visa brought down their rates somewhat a few months ago. The retail chains and gasoline companies simply ignored the complaints and the advice of the parliamentary committee. They are ripping off the public.
There are other groups which have done a much better job than the ones I have already mentioned. For example, credit unions in Saskatchewan and Ontario are offering a Mastercard tied to the over-draft rate of 12.5 per cent. This is 6.1 per cent less than the other credit card companies charge, except Canada Trust which recently cut its rate. As well, they charge no other fee. The credit card companies touted out all manner
August 25, 1987

of excuses for not being able to cut rates. Eiowever, as I indicated, they did cut rates a fraction back in February. Just as soon as the bank rate went up a few weeks ago, the companies began to increase their rates.
The parliamentary committee which studied the question made a number of recommendations. I would like to refer to one, one to which the Minister of State for Finance should pay attention. This recommendation appears in the report of the parliamentary committee and is dated March, 1987. It is the committee's sixth recommendation. It states that although the committee recommends that ceilings on interest rates not be imposed at this time, present money market rates indicate that there should be a substantial downward movement in credit card interest rates and other related charges. In the event that major Schedule A banks do not take action, at least to the extent of the action taken by the Toronto-Dominion Bank, then the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) should investigate to determine if there is anticompetitive behaviour and take appropriate action.
I can tell the Minister what the action should be. The State Treasurer of the State of Illinois took action. He wrote to five or six of the major banks in his state, asking them to lower their interest rates. He told them that if they did not, he would move the state funds which the banks held to other banks. They complied and interest rates in February of this year in that state were at 13.8 per cent. Not only that, the Treasurer introduced a Bill into the State Legislature which provided for an amendment to an Act in relation to the rate of interest. It imposes a ceiling on credit card revolving credit interest rates at the amount of 3 per cent over the prime rate established by the largest bank in Illinois. It provides for such a rate to be adjusted every six months.
We could take the same action here. We could introduce legislation which would tie the interest rates charged to people who do not pay their unpaid balances when they receive their statements to a fixed percentage over the interest rate set by the Bank of Canada.
This is an important matter. Members of Parliament, people who are in the upper-income brackets who use credit cards, pay whatever balance they owe when they receive their statements. They are able to do that. But there are hundreds of thousands of Canadians who find that they cannot do that, and they let it ride. They are being hit with charges of anywhere from 18 per cent to 28 per cent. That is reprehensible. It ought not to be permitted. If the companies involved will not take action voluntarily, then I call upon the Government to bring in legislation which will prevent them from doing this.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bud Bradley (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: CORPORATE AFFAIRS-HIGH INTEREST RATES CHARGED TO CREDIT CARD USERS-INTERVENTION BY ILLINOIS STATE TREASURER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Hon. Member for his intervention in this regard. I should point out that the Hon. Member has raised an issue that has been discussed many times in the House, namely, the spread between the Bank of Canada rate and the other lending rates in the market-place.
Adjournment Debate
As the Hon. Member knows, on May 26, 1986, the House of Commons issued an order to the Finance Committee to study the present interest rates charged by credit card companies. The Finance Committee tabled its report in March of this year. The Government welcomes the report. At this time, I would like to commend the committee members for their efforts in reviewing this important topic.
The report contains seven recommendations. For most readers the report's principal findings would probably be that there was some room for the level of credit card interest rates to be reduced. Based on the information that was provided by the credit card companies, the House Finance Committee estimated that credit card companies could lower their charges to consumers by about 3 per cent through a combination of lower interest rates, user fees, and longer grace periods.
In April, the major banks lowered their customer charges along the lines of the report's recommendations. Some, but not all banks have recently announced that they will be increasing their credit card rates by just over .5 per cent in October. I would note that since April the prime rate has increased by 125 bases points, from 8.75 per cent to 10 per cent.
While there is undoubtedly a linkage between the bank rate and other interest rates, such as the chartered banks' prime lending rate and credit card interest rates, I would note that it is not an exact or inflexible relationship. The committee's report found that there is not a direct one-to-one relationship between short-term interest rates like the Bank of Canada rate, and the credit card rates. The rates charged by credit card companies reflect a number of considerations and influences. A change in the bank rate does not automatically warrant a change in the credit card rate.
The recommendations of the report deserve careful study. Hon. Members should note that several of the recommendations require federal-provincial consultations. In this regard, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) has established a working group with his provincial counterparts to review the whole issue of cost of credit card disclosure for all types of consumer lending, and the harmonization of federal and provincial requirements.
I believe that the House Finance Committee's report shows that credit cards perform a useful function, but that there is a need for more information so that consumers can take advantage of the existing competition in the market-place. 1 would remind the Hon. Member that the Government has already started the process of modernizing and strengthening our financial system.
On December 18, 1986, the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) tabled the policy paper entitled "New Directions for the Financial Sector". The proposals will allow more players into the market-place, which will benefit not only borrowers but also savers who provide funds to financial intermediaries.
